abstract: Flight is a remarkably efficient mode of locomotion that is largely responsible for the extraordinary evolutionary radiations of birds, bats, pterosaurs, and insects. Whereas walking animals need only control locomotion on a two-dimensional surface, flight requires active altitude regulation, a process by which the brain transforms self-motion cues into motor patterns that regulate lift. Using an integrative approach combining optogenetics, high-speed videography, two-photon imaging, robotics, and connectomics, we identified a single pair of descending neurons in Drosophila that control altitude. To search for candidate cells, we performed an optogenetic screen of sparse driver lines targeting descending neurons that project to the flight neuropil of the ventral nerve cord and identified one bilaterally paired neuron, DNa10, whose activation elicits changes in wing kinematics consistent with descent. A replay of the kinematics on a dynamically scaled robot confirmed that the wing motion elicited by DNa10 activation generates a reduction in upward force. Optogenetic activation of this neuron causes free-flying animals to descend, whereas ablation or silencing of the cell in tethered flies elicits fictive ascent. Functional imaging reveals that DNa10 is activated by downward visual motion and inhibited by upward motion. These results are consistent with a connectomic analysis showing that DNa10 receives monosynaptic input from large-field visual interneurons sensitive to vertical body motion and provides direct output to three wing motor neurons that regulate the lift. Collectively, these results identify core components of a circuit for altitude control that links the detection of visual motion to the alteration of aerodynamic forces.
